bill.title: Healthy H2O Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.
bill.officialSummary: Healthy Drinking Water Affordability Act or the Healthy H2O Act This bill directs the Department of Agriculture (USDA) to establish a program under which USDA awards grants for improving the quality of drinking water in certain rural areas. Grants may be given to individuals or entities, such as home owners, renters, and licensed child-care facilities, that have demonstrated the presence of one or more health contaminants in their drinking water. Grants may also be given to nonprofit organizations to help individuals and entities test their water, analyze the results of the tests, and reduce the contamination.

classification.plainSummary: This bill would create a new grant program run by the Department of Agriculture to help people in rural areas improve their drinking water quality. Grants would go to homeowners, renters, and childcare facilities that have tested positive for health contaminants in their water, as well as to nonprofit organizations that help people test their water and reduce contamination.

industries.rationale: The bill directly funds water quality testing and contamination reduction, creating new revenue opportunities for water treatment and testing service providers.
Grant-funded water quality improvements in rural homes and facilities would likely require installation of filtration systems and infrastructure work.
The program is administered by USDA and targets rural areas, which may include agricultural operations, though the bill focuses on residential and childcare facilities.

plain.whatItDoes: This bill would order the USDA to establish a program under which USDA awards grants for improving the quality of drinking water in certain rural areas.
plain.whoItTouches: People living near whatever is being regulated.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in the air, water and land where you live. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
